steps.body: A fraction starts with a **fair cut**. Cut a bar into pieces that all match, and each piece earns a name: half, third, fourth. Cut it into four random chunks? Those are just… chunks. Fairness is what makes the names mean something.

widget.prompt: Tap every bar that shows a FAIR cut into fourths.

hotspots.label: Bar B: four pieces, one much bigger
hotspots.feedback: Four pieces, yes — but they don't match. The big chunk isn't 'a fourth'; unfair cuts earn no names.

hotspots.label: Bar C: three matching pieces
hotspots.feedback: Beautifully fair — but that's a cut into THIRDS. Fourths need exactly four matching pieces.

widget.missFeedback: Fourths needs BOTH things: exactly four pieces AND all of them matching.
widget.successFeedback: Bars A and D pass: four pieces, all equal. B fails the fairness test; C fails the count.

predict.prompt: What makes a cut into fourths FAIR — having four pieces, or having four EQUAL pieces?

options.label: Four pieces with one big one

predict.reveal: Fourths only count when every piece matches — four pieces of different sizes is a cut, but it isn't fourths.

cml.actionGoal: Manipulate the model and track how it represents equal parts.
invariants: The manipulated model and the mathematical relationship for equal parts must stay consistent.
misconceptions: Changing a visible feature without preserving the relationship that defines equal parts.
cml.counterfactualPrompt: What change would make the model stop representing the same mathematical relationship?

explanationVariants: Thirds means three EQUAL shares — a giant piece and two slivers are three pieces, but none of them is 'a third.'
The name is a promise about size: every third of the same sandwich must be the same amount.

widget.prompt: A sandwich is cut into 3 pieces. When is each piece a THIRD?

options.label: Only when the 3 pieces are equal
options.feedback: Fair shares or no name — three matching pieces make thirds.

options.label: Always — three pieces means thirds
options.feedback: Cut one giant piece and two slivers: still three pieces, but calling a sliver 'a third' would break the name's promise. Equal is the rule.

options.label: Only if the sandwich is square
options.feedback: Shape doesn't matter — round pizzas, long subs, square pans all cut into thirds. EQUAL matters.

options.label: Never — sandwiches can't be thirds
options.feedback: Anything you can cut fairly can be fractioned. Three equal shares of a sandwich are thirds, deliciously.

steps.body: The **names come from the count**: 2 fair pieces make halves, 3 make thirds, 4 make fourths, 6 make sixths, 8 make eighths. Notice something sneaky: more pieces from the same bar means each piece gets SMALLER. Hold that thought — a whole chapter is coming for it.

explanationVariants: Six equal pieces → each is a sixth. The name simply reads the piece count.
Careful with cuts vs pieces: 5 snips across a ribbon make 6 pieces — the name follows the PIECES.

widget.prompt: A ribbon is fair-cut into 6 pieces. What is each piece called?

options.label: A sixth
options.feedback: Six equal pieces, each one a sixth — the count names the piece.

options.label: A fifth
options.feedback: The cuts-vs-pieces trap! It took 5 snips to make them — but there are SIX pieces, and pieces get the name.

options.label: A sixer
options.feedback: Close in spirit! The math name is 'sixth' — the same family as third and fourth.

options.label: A half
options.feedback: Halves come from a 2-piece cut. Six pieces are far finer — each is a sixth.

steps.body: Inspector round two: sort the cuts.

widget.prompt: Fair cut (pieces earn names) or unfair cut (just chunks)?

items.label: A bar in 3 pieces, one huge
items.feedback: The huge one breaks the match — three chunks, no names.

items.label: A circle in 4 matching wedges
items.feedback: Four equal wedges — fourths, round edition.

items.label: A square in 2 pieces, big and small
items.feedback: Two pieces that don't match aren't halves — a half must be exactly half.

widget.missFeedback: One test: do ALL the pieces match? Yes → names. No → chunks.
widget.successFeedback: Equal pieces earn names; unequal pieces are just chunks, whatever their count.

steps.body: But WHY the fuss about equal?
explanationVariants: A name like 'a fourth' is a promise: the same amount every time, for that whole. Unequal pieces would make the promise meaningless.
Fractions let us talk about amounts without measuring — that only works if the pieces are guaranteed to match.

widget.prompt: Why do fractions DEMAND equal pieces?

options.label: So a piece's name tells its true size — 'a fourth' must always mean the same amount of that whole
options.feedback: The name is a size guarantee. Equal pieces are what make the guarantee real.

options.label: To make the picture look tidy
options.feedback: Tidiness is a side effect. The real reason is the promise: anyone hearing 'a fourth' must know exactly how much that is.

options.label: They don't — close enough counts
options.feedback: Close-enough breaks everything downstream: comparing, adding, sharing. The equal rule is what makes fraction math trustworthy.

options.label: Because unequal pieces are impossible to cut
options.feedback: Unequal pieces are easy to cut — kitchens prove it daily! They're just not allowed to wear fraction names.

hints: Cuts and pieces are different counts.
Picture it: 1 cut makes 2 strips. 2 cuts make 3.
Each new cut adds exactly one more strip.
explanationVariants: Three cuts make FOUR strips (cuts + 1), all equal — so each strip is a fourth.
Walk it up: 1 cut → 2 strips, 2 cuts → 3 strips, 3 cuts → 4 strips. Pieces always beat cuts by one.

widget.prompt: Maya makes 3 straight cuts across a brownie pan, spacing them so all the strips match. How many equal strips does she get?

commonErrors.feedback: 3 counts the CUTS. Watch one cut make two pieces — every cut after that adds one more. Three cuts leave four strips.
6 doubled the cuts — but only the FIRST cut makes two pieces; each later cut adds just one. Count up: 2, 3, 4.

widget.fallbackFeedback: Start at one whole pan and add a strip per cut: 3 cuts → 4 strips.

takeaways: Fair cuts earn names; unequal pieces are just chunks.
The piece COUNT gives the name: 4 equal pieces → fourths.
Count pieces, not cuts — pieces always beat straight cuts by one.
steps.teaser: one piece is about to get famous: the unit fraction, the building block of everything.

concept.body: Quick rewind. The fairness test: **imagine stacking the pieces**. If every piece lines up exactly with every other, the cut is fair and the pieces earn a name. One piece pokes out? Chunks — no name.

explanationVariants: One bigger piece fails the stack test — the four pieces don't match, so none is 'a fourth.'
Fourths is a size promise; a mismatched piece breaks it for the whole set.

widget.prompt: A pie is cut into 4 pieces, but one is bigger than the rest. Are the pieces fourths?

options.label: Not fourths — the pieces don't match
options.feedback: The stack test fails, so the name is off the table. Four chunks, no fourths.

options.label: Yes — four pieces are always fourths
options.feedback: Count alone isn't enough. Stack them: the big one pokes out, and the name's size-promise breaks.

options.label: Only the big one is a fourth
options.feedback: Funny idea — but if pieces differ, NONE gets the name. Fourths describes a matching set.
